title: Living into Our Values
hook: The values list matters only after the chosen words become visible behavior.
counterintuition: Values are not alignment posters; they are tradeoff rules with slippery violations named in advance.
tryThisNow: Pick one stated value and write the behavior that would prove it under social pressure.
keyTakeaway: Values become real when people can see the behaviors that support or violate them.

breakdown.fastRead: Values become usable only when they are narrow enough to guide tradeoffs. A long list can sound inclusive while hiding the fact that no priority will win when pressure arrives. Living into values means naming the behaviors, costs, and tempting shortcuts attached to each word. Courage is visible when a leader refuses a discriminatory joke, enforces a boundary, or tells the truth at an approval cost. Values stop being decoration when they change what people do in uncomfortable moments. If a handoff fails, generosity can preserve intent while the agreement, owner, and impact still get named.
breakdown.deepRead: The values work becomes real only when words are translated into behaviors, slippery moments, and costs people can recognize before pressure arrives. The mechanism is specificity: a value guides action only after people can identify the conduct it demands. Organizations stop using values as wall decor and start using them as decision tools. Individuals can handle feedback and conflict with a clearer sense of what must be protected. Aspirational values do not shape culture until they are converted into specific behaviors people can practice, measure, and repair. Integrity means choosing courage over comfort and practicing values instead of merely professing them. A leader needs a very small number of core values because too many priorities become an escape from commitment. The organization names Be Brave, Serve the Work, and Take Good Care as operating priorities. Each phrase is tied to behaviors such as clear communication, boundaries, service, gratitude, and respect. Personal and professional values cannot be split without creating confusion about identity and decision-making. A value earns trust when it decides a tradeoff. Words become values only when behavior pays the cost. Generosity cannot replace a missing agreement.
breakdown.fullRead: Brown rejects decorative alignment. A leader has to decide which values travel across settings and what conduct proves them when approval is at risk. The shallow version is to pick inspiring words and assume alignment will follow. The real assignment is behavioral: name what the value looks like, name the tempting violations, ask for feedback, and accept that values become visible when comfort is at stake. The values work begins by rejecting vague aspiration. Integrity is defined behaviorally: choosing courage over comfort and practicing values instead of simply admiring them. The first task is narrowing. A long list of admirable words lets people avoid tradeoffs, so the exercise pushes toward two core values that can guide both professional and personal decisions. Splitting home values from work values is treated as a false division because identity travels across settings. Most organizations fail to make values teachable and observable, leaving employees with slogans instead of behavioral expectations. The second task is translation. A value must become teachable and observable, which means naming the behaviors that support it and the slippery behaviors that violate it under pressure. Slippery behaviors reveal where pressure pulls people away from their stated values. Courage, for example, can show up as refusing discriminatory humor or setting boundaries around hateful comments. The third task is sustaining values during feedback, privilege conversations, conflict, and exhaustion. Feedback tests values because defensiveness, blame, and self-protection become tempting exactly when learning is most needed. A long list can feel generous, but it often hides the absence of priority. The sharper practice asks which value will govern when two good things cannot both win. Once that choice is made, people need to know the behavior that proves it and the shortcut that violates it. The value also needs a cost test: if nobody risks disapproval, convenience, or status, the word may be admired without being practiced and remembered. The values work succeeds when the chosen word, visible conduct, and refused shortcut are all plain enough to guide a tense tradeoff. Empathy and self-compassion become protective practices because defensiveness often appears when values are tested. The arena seats for trusted empathy and self-compassion keep criticism from turning into shame or collapse.

examples.title: Offsite Narrowing

planSpec.audience: Gwen and leaders facing values offsite
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Values list narrowed to two to practice values into behavior in values offsite

examples.scenario: Monday at 8:45 a.m. during an executive values offsite. Gwen wants all twelve official values to stay on the offsite wall. The list feels inclusive, but it cannot settle a tradeoff if every word has equal weight.
examples.whatToDo: She narrows the list to the few values that can decide a hard tradeoff and records what each one costs.
examples.whyItMatters: The division gains guidance because Gwen chooses commitment over inclusive decoration.

examples.title: Conference Courage
tags: Courage shown through discriminatory jokes and social media boundaries

planSpec.audience: Hiro and leaders facing conference reception
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Courage shown through discriminatory jokes and social media boundaries to practice values into behavior in conference reception

examples.scenario: Thursday night at a sales conference reception. Hiro hears a discriminatory joke at a conference reception and knows silence would be easier. The courage value will either become behavior now or remain private agreement.
examples.whatToDo: He states the boundary in the moment and leaves the approval cost with the person who crossed it.
examples.whyItMatters: The value becomes visible because Hiro lets behavior, not private agreement, carry the proof.

examples.title: Manuscript Work
tags: Brene Brown Education and Research Group values

planSpec.audience: Ines and leaders facing manuscript review
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Brene Brown Education and Research Group values to practice values into behavior in manuscript review

examples.scenario: Tuesday at 1:30 p.m. in a research manuscript review. Ines watches manuscript feedback turn Be Brave into permission to attack. The value needs a behavioral definition before it becomes a shield for ego.
examples.whatToDo: She asks which comment serves the work and which comment is protecting the speaker's ego.
examples.whyItMatters: The research team keeps courage connected to care because Ines defines the value in conduct.

examples.title: Remote Boundary

planSpec.audience: Jonas and leaders facing remote operations
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Values list narrowed to two to practice values into behavior in remote operations

examples.scenario: Wednesday morning during a remote handoff review. Jonas's remote team assumes good intent while missed handoffs keep hurting clients. Generosity is present, but the broken agreement still needs a name.
examples.whatToDo: He keeps the generous reading and identifies the missed owner, due time, and client impact.
examples.whyItMatters: The handoff improves because Jonas refuses to let a generous story erase reliability.

examples.title: Forum Inclusion
tags: Courage shown through discriminatory jokes and social media boundaries

planSpec.audience: Keira and leaders facing online forum
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Courage shown through discriminatory jokes and social media boundaries to practice values into behavior in online forum

examples.scenario: Friday at 5:20 p.m. in a professional association forum. Keira moderates a professional forum where hateful comments are being defended as openness. Inclusion cannot be both a value and an optional courtesy.
examples.whatToDo: She removes the comments and explains the inclusion behavior the forum will enforce.
examples.whyItMatters: Members see that inclusion is a standard of conduct, not a word on the page.

examples.title: Audit Integrity
tags: Brene Brown Education and Research Group values

planSpec.audience: Lior and leaders facing audit preparation
planSpec.stakes: the team may confuse values into behavior with comfort, image, or avoidance
planSpec.requiredBeat: use Brene Brown Education and Research Group values to practice values into behavior in audit preparation

examples.scenario: Sunday afternoon beside a finance audit checklist. Lior prepares for an audit and knows pressure will tempt people into small shortcuts. The likely compromises are easiest to stop before they feel necessary.
examples.whatToDo: He names the likely shortcuts before the audit starts and ties each one to the value it would violate.
examples.whyItMatters: The finance team has a usable guardrail because Lior names slippery behavior before stress makes it attractive.

questions.prompt: A division president wants to keep twelve official values.
choices: Keep all twelve so nobody feels excluded.
Narrow to the few values that can govern tradeoffs.
Rotate values monthly to avoid hard choices.
questions.explanation: The values list forces commitment; keeping every word or rotating them avoids the hierarchy needed for hard tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: A regional manager hears a discriminatory joke at a conference reception.
choices: Stay quiet because the event is informal.
Laugh politely and address inclusion later.
State the boundary and refuse the joke even if approval drops.
questions.explanation: Courage becomes visible when behavior costs comfort; silence and polite laughter make the stated value disappear in the moment it matters.

questions.prompt: A research team uses Be Brave and Serve the Work during manuscript conflict.
choices: Ask which behavior serves the work and which one protects ego.
Use Be Brave as permission to attack the weakest draft.
Take Good Care by avoiding disagreement.
questions.explanation: Values need behavioral definitions; the wrong choices distort bravery or care.

questions.prompt: A remote team assumes positive intent while missed handoffs keep hurting clients.
choices: Assume good intent while naming the agreement that was missed.
Keep generosity vague so nobody feels blamed.
Stop trusting the team after the third miss.
questions.explanation: Generosity needs evidence and boundaries; vague kindness avoids the miss, while blanket distrust throws away useful intent.

questions.prompt: A moderator sees hateful comments in a professional association forum.
choices: Leave them up to prove openness to all views.
Move the thread where fewer members will see it.
Remove the comments because inclusion is behavioral, not decorative.
questions.explanation: A stated inclusion value becomes real through conduct; leaving hate visible or hiding it quietly fails the behavior test.

questions.prompt: A controller prepares the team for audit pressure.
choices: Wait until the audit starts before discussing pressure.
Name likely shortcuts and the value each would violate.
Tell people integrity matters and skip behavioral detail.
questions.explanation: Slippery behaviors need names before pressure arrives; waiting or using slogans gives people no usable guardrail.

questions.prompt: A leader separates home values from work values to avoid tradeoffs.
choices: Work values can contradict home values without consequence.
Private values count only when they are publicly admired.
Values travel across settings and should survive discomfort.
questions.explanation: Brown rejects divided values because identity travels; contradiction and public admiration both make values conditional.

questions.prompt: During feedback, a manager says values are obvious because posters list them.
choices: Translate each value into observable actions and slippery behaviors.
Trust the posters because everyone knows the words.
Ask employees to memorize the value list before feedback.
questions.explanation: A value is real only when it changes conduct; posters and memorization preserve words without proving behavior.

questions.prompt: A team chooses Take Good Care but has not defined the behavior.
choices: Let each person interpret Take Good Care privately.
Define how Be Brave, Serve the Work, and Take Good Care behave in meetings.
Use the value as praise after good outcomes only.
questions.explanation: Shared values need shared behavioral definitions; private interpretation and after-the-fact praise cannot guide conflict.

reviewCards.back: A short list can guide tradeoffs when pressure arrives. A long list often preserves agreement by avoiding priority.
People can name the behavior, the likely shortcut, and the cost of staying aligned. The word has to change a decision.

reviewCards.front: What proves courage as a value?
reviewCards.back: Courage becomes visible when behavior changes despite approval, ease, or convenience being at risk.

reviewCards.front: How should generosity handle missed agreements?
reviewCards.back: Keep the charitable reading, then name the commitment, owner, and impact. Good intent does not erase a broken handoff.

reviewCards.front: What keeps values work from becoming decoration?
reviewCards.back: Define the uncomfortable behaviors the value requires before stress arrives. Otherwise inspiring words can hide misalignment.

implementationPlan.title: Living into Our Values practice
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Choose the values that decide tradeoffs, define their behaviors, and name the shortcuts pressure will tempt.

ifThenPlans.context: A values list is too long to guide a tradeoff
ifThenPlans.plan: If every value seems equally important, then narrow the list until one priority can actually decide the next hard choice.

ifThenPlans.context: Casual behavior violates a stated value
ifThenPlans.plan: If a joke, comment, or shortcut crosses the value, then address the behavior immediately and name the standard.

ifThenPlans.context: Good intent is being used to ignore a missed agreement
ifThenPlans.plan: If generosity is hiding impact, then preserve the charitable reading and still name the broken commitment.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within one day, pick one value and write the meeting behavior that would prove it when approval is at risk.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For seven days, record moments when a value costs comfort; practice one boundary that makes the value observable.

memorableLines.text: A value earns trust when it decides a tradeoff.
Words become values only when behavior pays the cost.
Generosity cannot replace a missing agreement.
